seoTitle: Choosing a PhD Country in Europe: Funding, Supervision and Research Fit
title: Choosing a PhD Country in Europe: Funding, Supervision and Research Fit
content:
The country matters, but the project and supervisor matter more. Compare actual offers by their research fit, funding arrangements, working conditions and the cost of living in the city where you would study.

Compare projects before countries

Start by finding research groups that work on the question you want to investigate. Read a few recent papers, identify the methods they use and check whether they are recruiting. A country with an attractive funding system may still be the wrong choice if the project offers little connection to your interests or preparation.

Compare supervision as carefully as the topic. Ask how often the group meets, who supports day-to-day research and what facilities or data you would use. Where possible, speak to current doctoral researchers about their experience without assuming one person's account represents the whole university.

Understand the funding arrangement

A doctoral place may be an employment contract, a scholarship or an admission offer with no awarded funding. Check the written terms: duration, gross salary or stipend, tuition coverage, mandatory deductions and any teaching duties. Do not compare a taxable salary directly with a tax-free stipend or assume every advertised payment covers twelve months.

In the UK, an award covering Home tuition can leave an international fee difference. In Germany and the Netherlands, an employed doctoral researcher and an externally funded candidate can have different conditions. The individual offer is the useful document to compare.

Budget for the actual city

Use university accommodation information and current rental listings to estimate housing. Add insurance, utilities, transport, food, deposits and the cost of moving. Ask when the first payment arrives and whether funding includes relocation support. A national average is a starting point, not a reliable budget for a specific city.

Build a shortlist you can assess

  • Research question and supervision: why this group, and what would you learn?
  • Funding and duration: what is guaranteed in writing, and what remains conditional?
  • Working and study conditions: contract percentage, teaching, training and facilities.
  • Practical arrangements: housing, language, dependants and immigration requirements.
  • Longer-term direction: what experience would this project give you for your next step?

You do not need to choose an entire country's research system in advance. Apply to suitable opportunities, then compare the offers using the same questions. That makes the decision more concrete than choosing by rankings or a single headline salary.

Official information

  • DAAD: research and doctoral study in Germany
  • Find research opportunities through EURAXESS

A comparison you can actually use

Put two offers side by side before deciding which country looks more attractive. Record the research question, supervisor, appointment length, funding model, tuition coverage and estimated take-home support. Then add the practical conditions: access to equipment, relocation costs, teaching expectations and the city’s housing options. Mark anything unconfirmed rather than filling the gap with an assumption. If an offer depends on a later scholarship decision, keep it separate from guaranteed funding. The result is a comparison of real opportunities, not a ranking of countries.

Relevant listings and guides on NextApply

To see how these questions apply to a real listing, review Applications of Quantum Technologies CDT PhD 2027. Compare its stated requirements with your own preparation and check the official source before applying.

You can also browse University of Strathclyde on NextApply and the doctoral training programmes category. Listings and recruitment windows can change.
